claims.text: Silver can be introduced into a W–Cu composite by powder mixing followed by infiltration or sintering under an inert atmosphere.
Adding approximately 1–2 wt% Ag during consolidation will place Ag primarily at W–Cu interfaces.
Interfacial Ag addition will enhance the thermal conductivity of W–Cu composites.
Interfacial Ag addition will preserve the mechanical robustness of W–Cu composites.
Interfacial Ag addition will preserve the irradiation resistance of W–Cu composites under fusion-relevant conditions.
Temperatures up to approximately 1000 °C and moderate neutron fluxes are representative of near-plasma or high-heat-flux fusion components.
Localized Ag at W–Cu interfaces mitigates interfacial thermal boundary resistance.
Low-level Ag addition refines the local interfacial microstructure.
Reducing W–Cu interfacial thermal barriers improves heat transfer through the composite.
The proposed interfacial modification will improve heat transfer without compromising structural integrity.
The proposed interfacial modification will not compromise resistance to irradiation-induced defects.
Ag addition will increase steady-state thermal conductivity by approximately 10–15% relative to an otherwise comparable Ag-free W–Cu composite.
The Ag-modified composite will retain at least 90% of the reference composite's strength.
The Ag-modified composite will have irradiation tolerance comparable to that of the Ag-free reference.
The beneficial effect is expected only at Ag contents no greater than 2 wt%.
Ag contents no greater than 2 wt% will produce minimal phase formation at typical infiltration or sintering temperatures.
Excessive Ag or inappropriate processing may form brittle intermetallic phases that reduce mechanical integrity and offset conductivity gains.
The supplied evidence contains no direct experimental study confirming Ag doping of W–Cu for improved thermal conductivity.
